questions.q: What is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose?
questions.why: NAC replenishes glutathione and prevents hepatic necrosis, ideally started within 8 hours.

questions.q: Which lab pattern fits SIADH?
questions.correct: Low serum osmolality with urine osmolality above 100 mOsm/kg
wrong: High serum osmolality with maximally dilute urine
Low serum osmolality with urine sodium below 10
Normal serum osmolality with urine osmolality below 50
questions.why: In SIADH ADH keeps the urine inappropriately concentrated despite low serum osmolality, and urine sodium is usually above 40.

questions.q: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia risks which complication?
questions.why: Limit correction to about 8 mEq/L per 24 hours in high-risk patients. Cerebral edema comes from rapid sodium falls, not rises.

questions.q: Which is the earliest ECG change of hyperkalemia?
questions.why: Peaked T waves come first, then PR prolongation, QRS widening and a sine-wave pattern.

questions.q: A patient has hyperkalemia with ECG changes. What is the first treatment to give?
questions.why: Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes. It does not lower potassium, so insulin with dextrose follows.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients?
questions.why: Primary hyperparathyroidism leads in outpatients. Inpatient hypercalcemia is usually malignancy, often through PTHrP.

questions.q: Which condition causes a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis?
questions.why: Bicarbonate lost in stool is replaced by chloride, so the gap stays normal. The other three add unmeasured anions.

questions.q: Visual blurring ('snowfield' vision) with a high anion gap acidosis points to which ingestion?
questions.why: Methanol is converted to formic acid, which injures the optic nerve. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase.

questions.q: Metabolic alkalosis with a low urine chloride (below 20) suggests which cause?
questions.why: Chloride-responsive alkalosis (vomiting, remote diuretics) has low urine chloride. Chloride-resistant causes have high urine chloride.

questions.q: Platelets fall from 250 to 90 on day 7 of heparin. What is the right management?
questions.correct: Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban
questions.why: HIT is prothrombotic, so stop every heparin source and anticoagulate with a direct thrombin inhibitor. Starting warfarin alone can worsen thrombosis.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis in the United States?
questions.why: Gallstones and alcohol are the two big causes. Triglycerides usually need to be above 1000 mg/dL to cause pancreatitis.

questions.q: A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or higher in ascites indicates which problem?
questions.why: High-SAAG ascites comes from portal hypertension (cirrhosis, heart failure). The three wrong options give a low SAAG.

questions.q: Which ascitic fluid count is diagnostic of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
questions.why: An ascitic PMN count of 250 or more is diagnostic even if cultures are negative. Treat with ceftriaxone and IV albumin.

questions.q: Which of these drugs is most associated with QT prolongation and torsades?
questions.why: Antipsychotics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron and methadone are the classic culprits.

questions.q: What is the first-line treatment for torsades de pointes?
questions.why: Magnesium works even with a normal level. Drugs that prolong the QT further (amiodarone, procainamide) make it worse.

questions.q: Which antibiotic most often raises the INR in a patient on warfarin?
questions.why: TMP-SMX inhibits CYP2C9 and warfarin metabolism. Rifampin and nafcillin induce metabolism and lower the INR.

questions.q: What is the best reversal for life-threatening bleeding on warfarin?
questions.correct: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K
questions.why: PCC works immediately and vitamin K sustains the effect. Protamine reverses heparin.

questions.q: Which agent reverses dabigatran?
questions.why: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal fragment that binds dabigatran. Andexanet reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.

questions.q: What is the most common ECG finding in pulmonary embolism?
questions.why: S1Q3T3 is classic but uncommon. Sinus tachycardia and nonspecific T-wave changes are far more frequent.

questions.q: A patient has a low pretest probability of PE. What is the next test?
questions.why: A negative D-dimer rules PE out when pretest probability is low. Imaging is for a positive D-dimer or a higher probability.

questions.q: A patient with PE is hypotensive and has right ventricular strain. What is the preferred treatment?
questions.why: Hemodynamically unstable PE gets thrombolysis (alteplase) unless it is contraindicated.

questions.q: Which drug class should be avoided in HFrEF?
questions.why: Diltiazem and verapamil are negative inotropes and worsen outcomes. The other three classes reduce mortality in HFrEF.

questions.q: Which exam finding is the most specific for heart failure?
questions.why: S3 is the most specific sign. Crackles and edema are common but have many other causes.

questions.q: Which IBD manifestation can lead to cholangiocarcinoma and is classically linked to ulcerative colitis?
questions.why: PSC runs independently of bowel activity and raises the risk of biliary cancer and colon cancer.

questions.q: Continuous mucosal inflammation that starts in the rectum describes which disease?
questions.why: Crohn disease has skip lesions and transmural inflammation. Ulcerative colitis is continuous and mucosal.

questions.q: Which lab pattern fits primary hypothyroidism?
questions.correct: High TSH with low free T4
wrong: Low TSH with low free T4
High TSH with high free T4
Low TSH with high free T4
questions.why: A failing thyroid gland raises TSH. Low TSH with low T4 points to a pituitary (central) cause.

questions.q: What should be given with IV levothyroxine in myxedema coma?
questions.why: Give steroids first because adrenal insufficiency can coexist and thyroid hormone speeds cortisol clearance.

questions.q: Which test is the most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.why: Anti-CCP is about 95% specific and can predict erosive disease. RF is also positive in many other conditions.

questions.q: Rheumatoid arthritis plus splenomegaly plus neutropenia is called what?
questions.why: Caplan syndrome is RA with pneumoconiosis nodules. Felty syndrome carries a risk of serious infection.

questions.q: Which supplement reduces methotrexate toxicity in rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.why: Folic acid lowers mucositis, cytopenias and liver enzyme elevation without losing much efficacy.

questions.q: A patient has septic shock. What is the initial fluid recommendation?
questions.why: Surviving Sepsis suggests 30 mL/kg of crystalloid within 3 hours for hypotension or lactate of 4 or more, then reassess.

questions.q: What is the first-line vasopressor for septic shock?
questions.why: Norepinephrine is first line. Vasopressin is added next, and dopamine is linked to more arrhythmias.

questions.q: Which infection classically causes eosinophilia?
questions.why: Tissue-invading helminths drive eosinophilia. Luminal protozoa usually do not.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of syncope?
questions.why: Reflex syncope is the most common, but cardiac causes carry the worst prognosis.

questions.q: Syncope on exertion plus a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur radiating to the carotids suggests what?
questions.why: Fixed outflow obstruction cannot meet demand during exertion. Exertional syncope with a murmur needs an echocardiogram.

questions.q: How is orthostatic hypotension defined?
questions.correct: A drop in systolic BP of 20 or more or diastolic of 10 or more within 3 minutes of standing
wrong: A drop in systolic BP of 10 or more within 30 seconds of sitting
A drop in systolic BP of 40 or more within 1 minute only
A rise in heart rate of 10 within 30 seconds
questions.why: Measure supine, then at 1 and 3 minutes standing. Absence of a heart-rate rise suggests neurogenic causes.

questions.q: Which is a common non-ACS cause of chronically elevated troponin?
questions.why: CKD, heart failure, myocarditis, PE and sepsis all raise troponin without plaque rupture.

questions.q: Muddy brown granular casts in the urine point to which diagnosis?
questions.why: AIN has white cell casts, GN has red cell casts, and prerenal azotemia has bland or hyaline casts.

questions.q: What is the 'triple whammy' that predisposes to AKI?
questions.correct: ACE inhibitor or ARB plus a diuretic plus an NSAID
wrong: Beta blocker plus statin plus aspirin
PPI plus calcium plus vitamin D
questions.why: The NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole and the ACE inhibitor or ARB dilates the efferent, which drops the GFR.

questions.q: Which vitamin prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy?
questions.why: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxine. Give B6 to at-risk patients such as diabetics and alcohol users.

questions.q: Which antibiotic is a classic cause of cholestatic drug-induced liver injury?
questions.why: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the most common cause of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury in many series.

questions.q: Which antihypertensive is notorious for causing constipation?
questions.why: Verapamil's effect on gut smooth muscle makes constipation common. Opioids and anticholinergics are the other big drug causes.

questions.q: Hypoglycemia with high insulin, high C-peptide and a negative sulfonylurea screen suggests what?
questions.why: Endogenous insulin comes with C-peptide. Exogenous insulin gives high insulin but low C-peptide.

questions.q: Classic fever of unknown origin is a temperature of 38.3 C or higher lasting at least how long?
questions.why: Classic FUO is at least 3 weeks of fever with no diagnosis after a week of evaluation.

questions.q: Who is most likely to have a myocardial infarction without chest pain?
questions.why: Diabetic neuropathy, older age and female sex all raise the chance of an atypical or silent MI.

questions.q: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by antibodies to what?
questions.why: Think of small cell lung cancer. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis.

questions.q: What must you check before starting an insulin infusion in DKA?
questions.why: Insulin drives potassium into cells. Replace potassium first if it is below 3.3.

questions.q: What is the first-line treatment for hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.why: Lactulose traps ammonia in the gut. Rifaximin is added for recurrence.

questions.q: What is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis?
questions.why: Epinephrine is the only drug that reverses anaphylaxis. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts.

questions.q: In the CHA2DS2-VASc score, what does the 'S2' stand for?
questions.why: Prior stroke, TIA or thromboembolism is worth 2 points. Age 75 or older is also worth 2.

questions.q: In CURB-65, what does the 'U' stand for?
questions.why: CURB-65 counts confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age 65 or older.
